Article.ArticleTitle: Clinical and genetic analysis of a family with 16p11.2 microduplication syndrome and variable multisystem manifestations.

Abstract.AbstractText: 16p11.2 microduplication syndrome (OMIM #614671) is a pathogenic recurrent copy-number gain at the 16p11.2 locus and is associated with variable expressivity across neurodevelopmental, growth, and medical phenotypes. Gastrointestinal symptoms have been reported in carrier cohorts, but detailed documentation of gastrointestinal motility and neuromuscular findings remains limited. We performed clinical and genetic analyses in a multigenerational family in which the proband (III1) presented with limb muscle pain, exercise intolerance, and chronic gastrointestinal symptoms. Next-generation sequencing (NGS), low-pass whole-genome sequencing (lpWGS)-based CNV analysis, Sanger sequencing, and qPCR validation identified a 0.8 Mb microduplication at 16p11.2 (BP4-BP5), involving 44 genes including TBX6, inherited from the mother (II2). The proband's clinical manifestations included developmental delay, pointed chin, low body mass index, gastrointestinal dysfunction (chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea, esophageal motility disorder, and rectal prolapse), forward-leaning gait, mild scoliosis, and limb muscle atrophy with inflammatory muscle involvement. Four family members (II2, III1, III2, and III4) carried the microduplication, but their available clinical features varied in severity and system involvement. The proband's twin brother (III2) had left ear deafness and epilepsy, individual II2 had blindness from cone-rod dystrophy, and III4 showed more pronounced scoliosis. This family provides a detailed clinical and genetic description of 16p11.2 microduplication carriers with prominent gastrointestinal motility and neuromuscular manifestations, thereby enriching the clinical characterization of this recurrent CNV and supporting substantial intrafamilial phenotypic heterogeneity.

Article.ArticleTitle: Retinal phenotypes and longitudinal clinical courses in patients with NPHP1-associated Senior-Løken syndrome.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aimed to describe retinal phenotype, longitudinal clinical course, and genetic findings in Japanese patients with NPHP1-associated Senior-Løken syndrome and their siblings.

This study included 12 patients with biallelic pathogenic NPHP1 variants, comprising 10 probands with symptomatic retinal dystrophy recruited from six ophthalmic centers across Japan and 2 affected siblings identified through family screening. Clinical and genetic findings were analyzed. Retinal dystrophy was diagnosed using fundus photography, fundus autofluorescence (FAF), optical coherence tomography, and electroretinography. Genetic testing was performed using whole-exome and/or whole-genome sequencing. Follow-up ranged from 0 to 44 years (mean, 14.6 years).
Retinal phenotype, onset of retinopathy and nephropathy, and genotype.

Retinal phenotypes included cone/cone-rod dystrophy (4 patients), retinitis pigmentosa (4 patients), sector retinitis pigmentosa (2 patients), pigmented paravenous retinochoroidal atrophy (1 patient), and normal retina (1 patient). FAF images showed a descending tract in 5 patients. Retinopathy preceded nephropathy in 9 patients, all of whom were initially diagnosed with Leber congenital amaurosis or early-onset retinal dystrophy. Genetic testing showed that 11 patients harbored a homozygous whole-NPHP1 deletion, whereas 1 carried compound heterozygous NPHP1 and EYS variants.

Patients with NPHP1-associated Senior-Løken syndrome showed considerable inter- and intrafamilial variability in retinal phenotype. Pigmented paravenous retinochoroidal atrophy can be associated with NPHP1 variants. A descending tract on FAF imaging may be a characteristic feature of retinal degeneration in Senior-Løken syndrome. Retinopathy, which commonly manifests as Leber congenital amaurosis or early-onset retinal dystrophy, often precedes nephropathy in patients with NPHP1-associated Senior-Løken syndrome.

Article.ArticleTitle: Comparison of raw-signal, feature-based and hybrid representations for machine-learning classification of retinal diseases from pattern electroretinography.

Abstract.AbstractText: Pattern electroretinography (PERG) is a non-invasive test of macular and retinal ganglion cell function, but its low amplitude and inter-subject variability limit its diagnostic use. This study compares three representations of the transient PERG waveform for the detection of six retinal and optic nerve conditions - Birdshot chorioretinopathy, cone-rod dystrophy, hereditary optic atrophy, macular dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa and Stargardt disease - against healthy controls, using the publicly available PERG-IOBA dataset. A total of 672 recordings from 336 examinations of 304 participants were preprocessed in six stages, and three representations were evaluated under one identical protocol: the raw 255-point amplitude-preserving waveform; 60 engineered clinical, spectral, wavelet and complexity descriptors; and a hybrid representation of 343 variables combining both, with multi-wavelet features from db4, sym2 and coif3. Performance was estimated by 10 × 5-fold participant-grouped cross-validation, in which both eyes and all repeat visits of an individual were kept in the same partition, with nested hyperparameter selection and all data-derived preprocessing fitted inside each training fold. Under the pre-specified primary classifier, the raw waveform gave the highest pooled out-of-fold AUC in four of the six classes (0.906 in cone-rod dystrophy, 0.842 in retinitis pigmentosa, 0.755 in macular dystrophy, 0.673 in hereditary optic atrophy) and the engineered descriptors in the remaining two (0.803 in Stargardt disease, 0.657 in Birdshot chorioretinopathy). The hybrid representation was highest in none, falling below the raw waveform in five of six classes by 0.002 to 0.018, and no non-linear classifier showed a hybrid advantage above 0.006 in mean AUC. A sensitivity analysis identified what does matter: removing the absolute amplitude scale by per-signal z-scoring cost the raw representation 0.055 AUC on average but the engineered descriptors only 0.023, and reversed the ordering of the three representations. Engineered descriptors did not improve on the waveform, but they made the problem tractable for linear models, which gained 0.128 in mean AUC from the reduction in dimensionality. These internally validated findings indicate that absolute PERG amplitude should be preserved rather than normalised away; participant-independent, multi-centre validation is required before clinical application.

Article.ArticleTitle: Phenotypic variability of a dominant CRX mutation and molecular insights into pathogenesis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Mutations in the cone-rod homeobox (CRX) gene cause dominantly inherited retinopathies with striking phenotypic variability. We define the clinical spectrum and molecular mechanism of a Class III CRX frameshift variant (c.590del, p.(Pro197Argfs*22); CRXP197Rfs) segregating in a four-generation family.

Six family members underwent genetic testing by a retinal dystrophy panel with Sanger confirmation. Carriers received longitudinal phenotyping, including visual acuity, fundus autofluorescence, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and full-field electroretinography (ffERG). Variant function was assessed by rhodopsin-promoter reporter assays in HEK293 cells and Crx-/- mouse retinal explants.

Three carriers shared the identical variant yet showed cone-rod dystrophy in variable severity and adult-onset ages. The proband developed progressive central vision loss, nyctalopia, outer-retinal atrophy, and reduced ffERG responses. Two carriers remained asymptomatic with preserved acuity and normal ffERG, exhibiting only mild outer nuclear layer thinning and abnormal autofluorescence. CRXP197Rfs lacked transactivation activity and suppressed wild-type CRX function in a dose-dependent manner.

CRXP197Rfs is a dominant-negative allele that produces cone-rod dystrophy with variable intrafamilial phenotypes. These findings caution against genotype-based prognostication and support mutant-allele knockdown with gene augmentation as therapeutic strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: The AP5B1 p.Leu785Pro variant is a frequent cause of late-onset macular dystrophy with variable extraocular manifestations.

Abstract.AbstractText: Inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) represent a large group of genetically heterogeneous disorders that often cause progressive visual loss. The fifth adaptor protein (AP-5) complex, which contributes to endolysosomal trafficking and lysosomal homeostasis, has previously been implicated in neurodegenerative syndromes, and more recently, bi-allelic variants in three of its subunits were found in families with macular dystrophy, including four with variants in AP5B1. Here, we describe 22 affected individuals from 20 families with AP5B1-associated IRD, all carrying the recurrent missense variant c.2354T>C (GenBank: NM_138368.5) (p.Leu785Pro), either in the homozygous state (16 families) or in trans with another rare heterozygous AP5B1 missense or loss-of-function variant. Five families were of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry and 15 families of European ancestry. Clinically, affected individuals presented with a predominantly late-onset macular dystrophy that frequently progressed to cone-rod degeneration. Characteristic retinal findings included foveal sparing, early peripapillary involvement, and a reticular pattern best observed by fundus autofluorescence imaging in the mid- or peripheral retina. The typical presenting symptom was decreased visual acuity. Age at onset ranged from 27 to 74 years, with most individuals becoming symptomatic after the fifth decade of life. Some individuals also presented with extraocular manifestations, most notably hearing loss, which was reported in 8 affected individuals. These findings further support AP5B1 as a cause of macular dystrophy, identify p.Leu785Pro as a relatively frequent pathogenic allele in individuals of European and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, and expand the associated phenotypic spectrum to include both isolated macular dystrophy and possible syndromic presentations.
